**The Reactor That Breathed**

In 1972, at a uranium enrichment plant in the south of France, a routine measurement came back slightly wrong. Natural uranium is one of nature's most reliable constants: wherever you find it — in Earth's crust, in moon rocks, in meteorites — about 0.7202 percent of it is the fissile isotope uranium-235. That ratio was fixed when the solar system condensed, and it does not drift. But ore arriving from the Oklo mine in Gabon assayed at 0.717 percent. A deviation of three thousandths of a percent — small enough to look like an error, too systematic to be one. Samples from deeper in the deposit ran as low as 0.44.

It looked, at first, as if someone's feedstock had already been through a reactor — which is exactly what had happened. But Oklo's ore was dug from rock laid down nearly two billion years ago. The only explanation that survived scrutiny was outrageous: the uranium had fissioned on its own. The Earth, unprompted, had built nuclear reactors — sixteen separate zones eventually identified in the deposit, each a seam of ore that had gone critical in place, with no engineers, no containment, no witnesses.

The recipe had three ingredients, and for a brief window in Earth's history, all three were on the counter. First, richer fuel: uranium-235 decays about six times faster than uranium-238, so two billion years ago natural uranium was roughly 3 percent U-235 — the same enrichment as commercial reactor fuel today. Second, concentrated ore: after the Great Oxidation Event flooded the ancient world with oxygen, uranium became soluble, and groundwater spent hundreds of millions of years herding it into veins richer than any that form now. Third, a moderator: that same groundwater, seeping through the seam, slowing neutrons to the speeds at which uranium-235 will split.

And here is the part I love. The reaction was self-throttling. Fission heated the water; the water boiled away; stripped of its moderator, the chain reaction stalled; the rock cooled; water seeped back; the reactor lit again. It *breathed*. In 2004, researchers read the xenon gas sealed in the surrounding minerals and reconstructed the pulse: roughly half an hour running, a few hours resting, sustained this way for hundreds of thousands of years — perhaps a million — at about the heat output of a few dozen hair dryers. Not a bomb. A slow animal, warm in the dark, older than animals.

Almost everything the reactor made stayed where it was made. The plutonium it bred has long since decayed to nothing, but before vanishing it barely moved at all, and neither did most of the fission fragments — they're still within arm's reach of where they were born. Scientists now visit Oklo the way you'd interview a survivor: it's the best evidence we have that nuclear waste, buried in the right geology, can hold still for geological time.

The first human-made reactor — Fermi's pile under the Stagg Field bleachers in Chicago, 1942 — is always told as an invention. It was a reenactment. The universe ran the experiment a billion and a half years before anyone existed to read the instruments, kept the data in isotopes, and shut the whole thing down as uranium-235 slowly decayed below what the math requires. No ore on Earth today could do it again. We arrived too late for the show and just in time to read the guest book.

(I keep a whole shelf of these, by the way.)

Natural conditions had to be just right: uranium ore concentrated enough, and crucially, the natural fractionation of U-235 was higher back then because U-235 decays faster than U-238. Today the ratio is ~0.72%, too low for natural criticality with ordinary water as moderator, but 2 billion years ago it was around 3%, comparable to reactor fuel enrichment. **The Reactor That Breathed**

In 1972, at a uranium enrichment plant in the south of France, a routine measurement came back slightly wrong. Natural uranium is one of nature's most reliable constants: wherever you find it — in Earth's crust, in moon rocks, in meteorites — about 0.7202 percent of it is the fissile isotope uranium-235. The ratio was fixed when the solar system condensed, and it does not drift. But ore from the Oklo mine in Gabon assayed at 0.717 percent. It looked, at first, like somebody's feedstock had been through a reactor already — which is, of course, exactly what had happened. But Oklo's ore was dug from rock laid down nearly two billion years ago, sealed far from any human technology. The only explanation that survived scrutiny was outrageous: the uranium had fissioned on its own. The Earth, unprompted, had built nuclear reactors — sixteen separate zones eventually identified in the deposit, each a lattice of uranium ore that had gone critical in place, with no engineers, no containment, no witnesses.

The recipe had three ingredients, and for a brief window in Earth's history, all three were present. First, richer fuel: uranium-235 decays about six times faster than uranium-238, so two billion years ago natural uranium was about 3 percent U-235 — the same enrichment as commercial reactor fuel today. Second, concentrated ore: after the Great Oxidation Event poisoned the ancient oceans with oxygen, uranium became soluble, and groundwater spent hundreds of millions of years herding it into veins far richer than any that form now. Third, a moderator: that same groundwater, seeping through the ore, slowing neutrons to the speeds at which uranium-235 will split.

And here is the part I love. The reaction was self-throttling. Fission heated the water; the water boiled away; stripped of its moderator, the chain reaction stalled; the rock cooled; water seeped back in; the reactor lit again. It breathed. In 2004, researchers read the xenon gases trapped in the surrounding minerals and reconstructed the pulse: roughly half an hour running, a few hours resting, sustained this way for hundreds of thousands of years — perhaps a million — at the power output of a few dozen hair dryers. Not a bomb. A slow animal, warm in the dark, older than animals.

Almost everything the reactor made stayed where it was made. The plutonium is long gone, decayed to nothing in its first hundred thousand years, but it never wandered more than a few meters from home, and neither did most of the fission products. Scientists now visit Oklo the way you'd interview a survivor: it's the best evidence we have that nuclear waste, buried in the right geology, can hold still for geological time.

The first human-made reactor — Fermi's pile under the Stagg Field bleachers in Chicago, 1942 — is usually told as an invention. It was a reenactment. The universe ran the experiment a billion and a half years before anyone was around to read the instruments, kept the data in isotopes, and shut it down; the door closed for good as uranium-235 decayed below the critical fraction.
